A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BDetCLIP and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, algorithms, and Appendices A–F. Corresponding material can be reliably matched despite reformatting and added experiments.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix E report original detection AUROCs, inference timings, prompt ablations, classification accuracy, and attack success rates.

after.justification: The original empirical results are retained, with additional attack evaluations, ImageNetV2 results, and prompt-generation performance and cost measurements.

M1.justification: The core contrastive detector remains. Appendix E explicitly adapts it to Bai et al.'s learned-prompt BadCLIP by combining learned context with random text in the malignant prompt. Appendix B also revises the written threshold rule; these changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Alongside the retained datasets and attacks, v2 evaluates ImageNetV2, Liang et al.'s dual-embedding BadCLIP, Bai et al.'s prompt-learning BadCLIP, and sample-specific ISSBA triggers. This substantially expands coverage beyond the original conventional visual-trigger scenarios, including learned prompts targeting Face on Caltech-101.

E2.justification: Matched detection comparisons retain STRIP, SCALE-UP, and TeCo; the backdoor-ratio analyses still compare against SCALE-UP alone. Added attack and dataset comparisons reuse these detectors. CleanCLIP supplies a repaired-victim condition, rather than an additional detector baseline.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce repaired versus unrepaired BadCLIP victims, a ViT16/Face configuration for learned prompts, and alternative prompt generators. Existing splits, poisoning procedures, backdoor ratios, and AUROC/timing metrics remain. Newly stated default architecture and sample counts document existing settings rather than establish protocol revisions.

E4.justification: Table 6 adds a substantive compatibility analysis testing detection before and after CleanCLIP repair. Appendix E additionally examines dependence on the prompt-generating language model and measures prompt-preparation costs. These extend the practical robustness and efficiency analyses beyond the retained prompt-count, prompt-length, component, and backdoor-ratio studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. The existing empirical density plots are retained, without a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Most matched results are identical, but Table 2 swaps STRIP's Food-101 BadNet/Blended AUROCs from 0.244/0.893 to 0.893/0.244. Added results include BDetCLIP AUROCs of 0.694 on Liang et al.'s BadCLIP versus STRIP's 0.794, 0.909 after CleanCLIP repair, 0.977 on Bai et al.'s BadCLIP versus STRIP's 0.987, 0.927 on ISSBA, and 0.931 average on ImageNetV2. Prompt-generation results are also added; these are new conditions, not version-to-version performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix B, Equation 8, replaces an expression mixing class and clean-sample indices and lacking class aggregation with the minimum class-summed detection score over clean validation images. This corrects the mathematical threshold definition. No theorems or proofs are added; other equation changes primarily concern notation.

C1.justification: The abstract adds the explicit claim that existing pre-training and fine-tuning defenses are inapplicable in black-box settings. The central claims of pioneering inference-time CLIP detection, using contrastive prompting, and achieving favorable effectiveness and efficiency remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 adds an important applicability boundary: standalone detection struggles against Liang et al.'s BadCLIP. It interprets the repaired-model results as evidence of CleanCLIP compatibility and claims the composite is the strongest defense. Appendix E adds arguments about offline prompt generation and open-source alternatives, while Appendix B explains the false-positive-oriented threshold. Appendix F's original limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the default 400M-pretrained ResNet-50 CLIP, gives per-dataset test and backdoor counts, and specifies the 50,000-image timing workload. It also documents alternative prompt-generator versions and generation times/costs. Existing poisoning details, eight-GPU hardware disclosure, and repository links are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds both BadCLIP papers, newer CLIP defenses, and references supporting the new model and dataset experiments. Section 4.1 expands the distinction between sample detection evaluated by AUROC and model repair evaluated by ASR. ISSBA was already cited in v1; its evaluation, rather than the underlying cited work, is new.

P1.justification: Most prose and section order remain. v2 standardizes benign/malignant prompt terminology, expands the comparator and threshold explanations, separates experimental results into Section 4.2, and adds an ethics statement. It also updates authorship/contact information and changes numerical citations to author-year style.

P2.justification: v2 adds six tables covering attack/repair tests, prompt-generation costs, alternative generators, and ImageNetV2. It converts the narrow inference-time table into a horizontal full-width table, redraws Figure 1 to mark both encoders, corrects Table 2's descriptive headings, and restyles the document layout. Figures 2–4 retain their substantive content.

improvement.justification: The added BadCLIP tests expose a concrete weakness and investigate repair compatibility, improving the practical credibility of the evaluation. The corrected threshold definition, explicit sample counts, and prompt-generation costs improve reproducibility and transparency. These gains are tempered by sparse setup details for some added experiments and a 'most powerful' composite-defense claim broader than Table 6 establishes.
